strengths: Clear and well-motivated desiderata framework (C∞ smoothness, global domain, analytic closed-form inverse, tractable Jacobian, expressive parametrization), and the proposed constructions (cubic rational, sinh conjugation, cubic conjugation) genuinely satisfy all five simultaneously — a property Table 1 shows no prior scalar bijection family achieves.

Careful and complete mathematical treatment: Appendix A provides full derivations of the Cardano-based inverses, parameter bounds (e.g., -1 < λ < 8), numerical-stability tricks, and the radial-flow Jacobian via the matrix determinant lemma; the regularity-at-the-origin analysis of radial flows (Section 4.2) is a thoughtful treatment of a coordinate singularity that many papers would gloss over.

Broad and largely fair empirical evaluation: 1D stacks, 2D coupling flows, radial flows, CIFAR10, the UCI suite (with the spline baseline reproduced inside the authors' own framework to isolate the scalar-bijection effect), runtime/memory benchmarks (Appendix B.8), and a scientific application to φ⁴ lattice field theory including a Z₂-symmetric zero-mode bijection that prevents mode collapse.

The qualitative smoothness claims are backed by quantitative evidence in Appendix B.3 (second-derivative MSE ~1445× worse for splines; training-loss variance reduced ~20×), which strengthens the central smoothness argument beyond pictures.

Good reproducibility: hyperparameter tables, architecture details, parametrization formulas, seed counts (6 seeds with error bars), and public code (bijx library). Limitations and future work are honestly discussed, including the radial-flow angular-mass constraint and un-tuned hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate: the building blocks are standard (Cardano-solvable cubics, conjugation with monotone maps à la neural ODE/spline practice, radial transforms extending Rezende & Mohamed 2015). The novelty lies in careful composition and satisfying desiderata jointly rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The headline '1000× fewer parameters' claim is made on a 2D spiral target whose radial structure strongly favors the proposed radial flow; this advantage does not transfer to generic benchmarks, where gains are modest (0.12 bpd on CIFAR10 vs. an augmented RealNVP baseline, with no comparison to stronger modern image flows).

UCI results are mixed: the proposed variants underperform the reproduced spline on HEPMASS and MINIBOONE, and the best variant is a hybrid (spline+) that incorporates the competing method — undercutting the message that analytic bijections are a strict improvement over splines.

Expressivity constraints are restrictive: the algebraic construction forces deg d ≤ 2 for the tail polynomial and deg n ≤ 2, so the single non-trivial family is a one-parameter cubic rational; per-layer expressivity relies on stacking, and runtime scales linearly with stack count (up to ~1.5–2× spline training cost on CIFAR10 per Appendix B.8).

Radial flows are evaluated only in 2D (with an acknowledgment), and the Fourier angular dependence is only illustrated via a truncated 1D series; the higher-dimensional (spherical harmonics) extension is left as future work, so the significance of the radial-flow contribution is limited in scope.

The practical importance of C∞ smoothness is demonstrated mostly in low-dimensional or derivative-sensitive settings; on standard benchmarks (CIFAR10/UCI) the spline baseline is competitive, so the practical benefit of smoothness in mainstream applications remains partially asserted rather than established.

strengths: The paper clearly articulates five desiderata for scalar bijections (C∞ smoothness, unbounded domain, closed-form analytic inverse, tractable Jacobian, expressive parametrization) and shows that no existing construction satisfies all of them. The two construction principles (algebraic rationals with cubic-solvable inverses; conjugation with superlinear monotone maps) are simple, principled, and well-motivated.

The mathematical development is careful and correct as far as I can verify: bijectivity constraints for the cubic rational are derived rigorously (Appendix A.1, including numerical-stability considerations for Cardano's formula), the radial-flow Jacobian derivation via the matrix determinant lemma is clean, and the regularity constraint at the origin for radial flows is correctly identified and honestly discussed.

Empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive and well-designed: controlled drop-in comparisons where all methods share architecture and hyperparameters, 6-seed error bars, ablations over stack count, parameter sweeps, qualitative layer-by-layer visualizations, wall-clock cost analysis, and honest discussion of where baselines win (spline underperforms their reproduction on HEPMASS/MINIBOONE; end-to-end runtime up to 1.5–2× spline).

The radial-flow architecture is a genuinely nice idea: preserving angular direction yields geometric interpretability (mass moves along rays, never crosses), extreme parameter efficiency on radially structured targets (~3 orders of magnitude fewer parameters than coupling flows on the spiral), and the Fourier angular parametrization is an inspectable expressiveness knob.

The lattice field theory application is more than a token experiment: the Z2-symmetric zero-mode bijection for preventing mode collapse is a concrete, meaningful demonstration that the framework enables problem-specific design, and ESS improvements over spline/affine baselines on a 20×20 lattice are meaningful.

Strong reproducibility: a released library (bijx), a tutorial notebook, complete hyperparameter tables (Table 5), architecture details, and numerical implementation tricks (asymptotic forms, stable special functions).

Limitations are discussed candidly (radial flows limited to low dimensions, hyperparameters not per-method tuned, single-layer angular-mass constraints), and the smoothness claim is backed by concrete measurement (second-derivative MSE ratios, loss-variance reduction in Appendix B.3).
weaknesses: Absolute gains on standard benchmarks are modest and mixed. On CIFAR10 the improvement over the (somewhat dated) RealNVP baseline is ~0.12 bpd and far from modern SOTA; on UCI, the sinh and spline+ variants underperform the spline reproduction on HEPMASS and MINIBOONE, so the headline 'matches or exceeds spline performance' holds only on a subset of datasets.

The claimed 1000× parameter efficiency of radial flows is demonstrated only on low-dimensional (2D) targets with favorable radial structure. The angular-mass conservation constraint means single radial flows cannot represent general angular mass profiles, and the authors themselves note the required layer count may scale adversely with dimension. The generality of the radial-flow contribution remains unproven.

The practical benefit of C∞ smoothness over C^k splines is quantified mainly in one controlled 1D experiment (second-derivative MSE, loss variance). While suggestive, the downstream scientific impact of smoother derivatives is asserted more than demonstrated; a higher-dimensional case where spline non-smoothness demonstrably causes failure would strengthen the case.

Novelty is incremental: rational bijections, sinh-based smooth constructions, and conjugation are established tools (and the authors appropriately credit Rezende & Mohamed (2015) radial flows as the ancestor of their radial architecture). The contribution is a careful systematization and combination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Comparison to free-form flows (Draxler et al., 2024) is relegated to a brief mention in the conclusion; given that free-form flows remove the exact-invertibility constraint entirely, a comparison or at least deeper discussion of the trade-off space would be valuable.

Some empirical choices could confound comparisons: radial flows use a learning rate an order of magnitude higher than coupling flows (5×10⁻³ vs 4×10⁻⁴), and the CIFAR10 'RealNVP+' baseline deviates from the published architecture (ActNorm, GELU), so the 0.12 bpd gain is relative to a reimplementation rather than the published number.

Stack-count degradation at large N (training instability in Figures 3 and 4) suggests a real practical limitation of composing many small bijections, which is only partially addressed by hyperparameter discussion.
